newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO says talks make progress despite differences.
newsitem.headline: NATO says talks make progress despite differences.

text.p: NATO and Russia said on Sunday they had made progress in their latest round of talks on clearing the way for the alliance's planned expansion into former communist Europe, but said differences remained.

In a joint statement issued after talks in Brussels between NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and Russian Foreign Secretary Yevgeny Primakov the two sides said they had agreed to meet again soon in Moscow.

"The talks took place in a constructive atmosphere. Progress is emerging although differences remain," the statement said, adding the two sides had tasked senior officials to start working on the next round "as early as tomorrow".
No details of the talks, which lasted less than the slated four hours, at Solana's private residence in Brussels were made available.
The meeting, the second in five weeks between Primakov and Solana, was part of a frenzied round of diplomatic activity in which the West hopes to overcome Moscow's objections to NATO's enlargement.

Before they began, Russian President Boris Yeltsin renewed his attack on NATO's plans to give membership to some of Moscow's former satellites, but held out some hope an end to the bitter wrangle between the former foes was now in sight.
He said he thought a compromise would be reached at a summit next month with U.S. President Bill Clinton.
"We have agreed to look for a compromise and I think we will find this compromise at the summit we are holding with President Clinton on March 20-21 in Helsinki," he told reporters.

Yeltsin, who discussed the issue with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright in Moscow last week, said his country's aim was to stall enlargement for as long as possible and "not allow the renewal of confrontation".
His remarks appeared to confirm the view of several alliance diplomats who say that, despite Moscow's strident public rhetoric, they detected a wish by Russia to start real negotiations.

Diplomats said they expected the discussions now to focus on guarantees sought by Russia that no weapons or troops would be stationed on the territory of possible new members, led by Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
"The Russians want that commitment in a legal document, that is a tricky one for NATO. But the important thing here is that we are now in real dialogue," said one senior diplomatic source.

Moscow's opposition to NATO enlargement was stressed again on Sunday by Defence Minister Igor Rodionov who said the army was heading for financial ruin and the West might therefore try to place Russia's nuclear arsenal under United Nations control.
"NATO is making every effort to deprive Russia of its strategic nuclear forces," Rodionov was quoted as telling veterans.

NATO diplomats said that, after weeks of allied concessions from arms control to offers of close military cooperation, Solana had planned to go on the offensive and try to get Primakov to offer something in return.
Primakov was due to leave early on Monday but his deputy Nikolai Afanasievsky would remain, possibly for detailed discussions with NATO Assistant Secretary-General Gebhard von Moltke.

Russia has made clear it wants a legally-binding treaty to govern its relations with NATO, while NATO prefers a more flexible political agreement which would not need ratifying by member states' parliaments.
